translationRepairs: Murong De named him Chao, made him Prince of Beihai, palace attendant, vanguard general, metropolitan commandant, with full staff.

Murong De named him Chao, enfeoffed him as Prince of Beihai, and appointed him Palace Attendant, General of the Agile Cavalry, and Colonel Director of Retainers, with authority to open an office and appoint his own staff.
The proposal correctly identifies the cavalry command but leaves several surrounding offices compressed or mistranslated.

De treated him with great courtesy, for the first time naming him Chao, enfeoffing him Prince of Beihai, appointing him palace attendant, chief general of the vanguard, colonel director of the retainers, opening an office and installing aides.

De treated him with great courtesy, first gave him the name Chao, enfeoffed him as Prince of Beihai, and appointed him Palace Attendant, General of the Agile Cavalry, and Colonel Director of Retainers, with authority to open an office and appoint his own staff.
The proposal fixes 驃騎大將軍; the revised sentence also renders the complete sequence of appointments in grammatical English.
Chao also deeply grasped De’s intent: within he gave full joyful service; without he humbled himself to men of talent—thereupon inside and outside praised his beauty.
Chao also deeply grasped De’s intent: within he gave full joyful service; without he humbled himself to men of talent—thereupon inside and outside praised his excellence.
Here 美 denotes merit or excellence, not physical beauty.
Later Murong Zhong held Qingzhou, Duan Hong Xu, and Gongsun Wulou mixed martial guard and palace cavalry roles at court.

Later Murong Zhong was appointed Inspector of Qing Province, Duan Hong Inspector of Xu Province, and Gongsun Wulou General of the Martial Guard while concurrently serving as Colonel of Encamped Cavalry and participating in court affairs.
The proposal separates Duan Hong from Xu Province but still leaves the offices unclear; the revision restores all three appointments.
Murong Chao heard and never forgave him.
When Chao heard of it, his anger and resentment showed in his words and expression.
恚恨形於言色 describes visible anger at that moment, not a permanent refusal to forgive.
Murong Fa skipped the funeral; Murong Chao sent a rebuke.
When Murong De died, Murong Fa again failed to attend the mourning rites, so Chao sent envoys to reproach him.
The revision restores De's death and the repeated dereliction marked by 又 while keeping the referents explicit.
General Feng Rong defected to Wei.
General of the Gentlemen of the West Feng Rong fled to Wei.
西中郎將 is a specific military office; the proposed word order is not idiomatic English.
Duke Zhuang’s minister Qumi was torn apart—recorded in the Annals.
Qumi, minister to Duke Zhuang of Zheng, was executed by chariot-tearing, as recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The historical gloss correctly identifies Qumi's ruler; the revision keeps that useful identification while stating the punishment and chronicle clearly.
Shizong when he capital at Qi also pitied that punishments missed the mean and sighed, forgetting food and sleep.
When Shizong made Qi his capital, he too lamented that punishments had lost their proper measure, sighing over it even as he ate and slept.
The proposal supplies the missing verb, but the complete revision also renders 失中 and 咨嗟寢食 naturally.
Yao Xing held Murong Chao’s women hostage, demanding vassalage, the imperial musicians, or else a thousand southerners.
Yao Xing detained Murong Chao's mother and wife, demanding that Chao declare himself a vassal and surrender the Grand Music performers; failing that, he was to send a thousand people from Wu.
超母妻 identifies the two hostages, while 吳口 means people from Wu and does not itself say they were captives.
Chao sent his vice director Zhang Hua and attendant for miscellaneous purposes Zong Zhengyuan to Chang’an, delivering a hundred twenty Grand Music performers to Yao Xing.
Chao sent his Vice Director Zhang Hua and Supervising Secretary Zong Zhengyuan to Chang’an, delivering a hundred twenty Grand Music performers to Yao Xing.
Supervising Secretary is an established rendering of 給事中 and removes the misleading generic paraphrase.
‘Now the Zongzhang goes west—surely the surplus will return east; is this not the omen of fortune and disaster!’”
Now the Zongzhang musicians have gone west; surely You Yu will return east. Is this not an omen of fortune and disaster?"
由餘 is the Qin statesman You Yu. The leading single quote belongs to the Laozi quotation in the preceding unit, so retaining it here breaks the dialogue nesting.
‘Now the Zongzhang goes west—surely the surplus will return east; is this not the omen of fortune and disaster!’”
Now Zongzhang has entered the west; surely You Yu will return east. Is this not the sign of fortune and disaster?"
The literal translation must restore the personal name and close Zhang Hua's speech without reopening the already closed Laozi quotation.
He rewarded the raiders with county duchies.
Chao reviewed the merits of the Suyu campaign and enfeoffed Huguti and the others as commandery and county dukes.
The existing translation omits the ruler, campaign, and named beneficiary; 郡、縣公 refers to dukedoms at commandery and county rank.
Another raid took Jinan’s governor and slaves.
He again sent Gongsun Gui and others with three thousand cavalry to raid Jinan, capture Administrator Zhao Yuan, and carry off more than a thousand men and women.
The source names the commander and administrator and describes abducted people, not slaves.
Liu Yu reached Dongguan; Murong Chao sent fifty thousand under Duan Hui and Helailu to Linqu.

That summer, the imperial army encamped at Dongguan. Chao sent six generals, including his Left Army commander Duan Hui and General Who Assists the State Helailu, with fifty thousand infantry and cavalry to occupy Linqu.
等六將 means six generals in total, not Duan Hui, Helailu, and six others; the revision also preserves their offices and the mixed force.
But from antiquity when begging aid, if you do not send a great minister you do not draw heavy troops—therefore Zhao’s thrice begging indentured no Chu army;
From antiquity, when seeking aid, failure to send a senior minister has meant failure to obtain a large relief force. Thus Zhao petitioned three times, yet no army came from Chu;
The proposal removes the nonsensical 'indentured' but remains awkward; the surrounding contrast is between Zhao's three failed appeals and the Lord of Pingyuan's successful embassy.
Before long, Liu Yu's army surrounded the city on all sides.
The sentence does not repeat Guanggu by name; retaining Liu Yu makes the acting force unambiguous.
Yao Xing dispatched Yao Qiang with ten thousand men to Luoyang to reinforce Han Fan.
At that time Yao Xing sent his general Yao Qiang with ten thousand infantry and cavalry to accompany Han Fan to Luoyang, join forces with Yao Shao, and come to the rescue.
The revision restores Yao Shao and the sequence in which Yao Qiang accompanied Han Fan to combine forces at Luoyang.
Murong Chao’s archers drove Zhang Gang back.
Chao grew angry and had concealed crossbowmen shoot at Zhang Gang, forcing him to withdraw.
伏弩 indicates crossbowmen placed in concealment; naming Zhang Gang resolves the proposal's ambiguous pronouns.
Right Vice Director Zhang Hua and palace secretary Feng Kai were both captured by Yu’s army.
Right Vice Director Zhang Hua and the Palace Aide to the Censor-in-chief Feng Kai were both captured by Yu’s army.
中丞 here is the censorate office Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, not a palace secretary.
In youth he had judgment and capacity; joy and anger did not show on his face; his wit was bright and hair splendid, his speech clear in debate.
Even in youth he had discernment and breadth; joy and anger did not show on his face, his intelligence and bearing were outstanding, and his speech was lucid and persuasive.
機神秀發 praises exceptional intelligence and presence; the revision removes the false reference to hair and gives the whole sentence grammatical form.
On that account, whether government was great or small, all was delegated to him; he thereupon became a founding assistant without [parallel] merit.
Thus all affairs of government, great or small, were entrusted to him, and he became a founding statesman of the first rank.
An independent witness preserves the expected reading 佐命元勳; the chapter's 無勳 is a transcription error that makes the clause self-contradictory.
His grandfather Feng Jun was a general.
His grandfather Feng Quan was a general.
悛 is read Quan; Feng Jun is a romanization error.
His grandfather was Jun, General Who Rouses Might.
His grandfather was Quan, General Who Rouses Might.
The literal field has the same erroneous reading of 悛 and should use Quan.
Murong Chao squandered Murong De’s legacy, provoked Jin, and destroyed the state.

Murong Chao inherited an established realm and a hegemon's legacy, yet neglected government and justice, delighted in hunting, shut out loyal men, advanced flatterers, and alienated his meritorious kin. His predecessors' legacy soon collapsed and his house's reputation went unrestored: he lost Suyu and brought disaster upon himself, opened Daxian to the enemy, and ended with ruler and ministers captive and the ancestral temples in ruins.
The proposal removes one unsupported polity name but still omits nearly the entire historian's judgment; the revision restores its concrete charges and consequences.
